text: Every chapter in this course solved one piece of a single, larger problem: what actually happens between a rider tapping "request ride" and a driver showing up. This capstone puts the pieces back together. One simulated request will pass through geospatial indexing, dispatch matching, routing and pricing, the trip state machine, the event backbone, the service mesh, distributed tracing, and the Docstore storage layer — in that order, for real reasons, each stage inherited from a chapter that derived it from first principles rather than asserted it. Then you'll break individual stages, one at a time, and watch the exact recovery mechanism each earlier chapter built actually engage.

You will be able to Trace one rider request through every layer of Uber's backend, in the correct order, and explain why that order is forced. You will understand Why no single stage in this pipeline can be understood in isolation — each one's guarantees depend on the stage before it. You will predict Where a broken stage's failure gets absorbed — a mesh retry, an event-bus backlog, or a regional failover — and why it's absorbed there and not elsewhere. You will simulate The full request end to end, break any single stage on purpose, and watch the rest of the system respond exactly the way chapters 1–17 taught you it would.

From a rider's perspective, requesting a ride is a single tap. From a systems perspective, that tap triggers a chain of distinct, individually hard problems, each of which this course spent a full chapter deriving: where is this rider, right now, in a form a computer can search efficiently (chapter 2)? Which of the nearby drivers should be assigned, given that drivers can't be double-booked and greedy nearest-first matching produces worse outcomes than a batched assignment (chapter 4)? What's the real ETA along actual roads, not a straight line (chapter 5)? Does current supply/demand justify a price above the base fare (chapter 6)? How does the trip's state advance reliably across multiple services without double-charging anyone (chapter 7)? And underneath every one of those questions: how do the services answering them actually find and call each other reliably (chapter 9), react to each other's events (chapter 10), get observed when something goes wrong (chapter 11), and durably store the result (chapters 14–17)?

None of those sixteen prior chapters can be fully understood in isolation — each one's guarantees are a precondition for the next stage's correctness. This chapter's entire purpose is to make that dependency chain concrete, in the order it actually executes, for one real request.

This is a synthesis, not a new topic. Nothing here contradicts or replaces chapters 1–17 — every mechanism used below is the exact mechanism its originating chapter derived, cited by name. Where this chapter shows a specific pipeline order or a specific simulated timing number, it is an illustrative, first-principles reconstruction of how these pieces fit together — not a claim about any single company's exact current internal request path, which is not public in that level of detail for any ride-hailing company, Uber included.
Every milestone below was covered in an earlier chapter. Seeing them on one shared timeline is the point of a capstone: this is one continuous engineering history, not seventeen unrelated stories.

UberCab's 2009 founding and 2010 San Francisco launch, the real 2013–14 New Year's Eve surge-pricing backlash, the 2014–15 microservices migration era, Ringpop and TChannel's 2015 open-source release, the real 2016 "Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL" blog post and its public reception, Jaeger's open-source release and 2017 donation to the CNCF, and H3 and M3's 2018 open-source releases are all real, publicly documented facts this course has drawn on throughout. Where any chapter showed a specific internal algorithm or parameter not on the public record, it said so plainly and taught the general technique instead — this capstone inherits that same discipline rather than suddenly claiming more certainty in the final chapter.

Before assembling the real pipeline, revisit the honest starting point chapter 1 and chapter 8 both opened with: what if the entire request were handled by one function, in one process, against one database?

This is exactly right as a first draft — it is legible, has no distributed-systems complexity at all, and for a company running in one city with a few hundred trips a day, it might never need to change.
Where every system starts. One process, one database, completely correct at this scale — this course never claimed otherwise.
The scale this course actually cares about. Nothing in the naive function changed — but every assumption it silently relied on (one geography, low concurrency, no real distance) stops holding.
Every chapter's failure mode, at once. These aren't sequential problems you hit one at a time — at real scale, all of them are live simultaneously, in the same naive function.
Verdict. The fix isn't one clever trick — it's exactly the sixteen chapters of decomposition this course already walked through, now assembled into one pipeline.

At Uber's actual scale — millions of trips per day, across thousands of cities — the naive monolith doesn't fail in one way, it fails in every way chapters 1 through 17 each identified independently, simultaneously:

Geospatial (ch. 2): a naive geohash bucket has an edge-boundary flaw — two physically adjacent points can land in wildly different buckets, silently missing nearby drivers. Dispatch (ch. 4): greedy nearest-first matching double-books drivers under concurrency and produces globally worse total wait time than a batched assignment. Pricing (ch. 6): a fixed base fare provides no mechanism to attract more drivers into a cell experiencing a real demand spike — riders simply can't get a car. Trip lifecycle (ch. 7): one synchronous database write with no state machine and no idempotency key means a retried request can double-charge a rider or double-create a trip. Scale and coupling (ch. 8, 9): one process handling every concern means one team's bug blocks every team's release, and there is no isolation between a slow dependency and the rest of the request. Storage (ch. 14–17): one database, one region, is both a latency floor for distant cities and a company-wide blast radius for any incident.

None of these failures are independent surprises — they are the same underlying fact (a system's simplest version is correct at small scale and fails in a specific, previously-derived way at Uber's real scale) showing up once per subsystem. The rest of this chapter is the assembled fix: the real pipeline that each chapter's "better solution" section built, now shown running together, in the order a real request actually executes it.

Every stage below is a direct citation of an earlier chapter's "final architecture." Step through the real order a request executes them in, and notice how each stage's output is a precondition for the next.

You cannot match a driver (chapter 4) before you know the rider's H3 cell (chapter 2) — matching needs a candidate set of nearby drivers, and "nearby" is exactly what the spatial index answers. You cannot price the trip (chapter 6) before a driver and route exist (chapters 4, 5) — surge is a multiplier on a base fare that routing helps determine. You cannot publish a trip-matched event (chapter 10) before the trip state machine (chapter 7) has actually advanced to "matched" — the event is a fact about a state transition that must have already happened. Every dependency here is a real data dependency, not a convention.

Every stage boundary is now a real network call. Chapter 9's entire argument — that thousands of services can't each hand-roll retries and timeouts — applies at full force to this pipeline: eight inter-service hops means eight places a sidecar's retry, timeout, and circuit-breaking logic has to be correct. End-to-end latency is the sum of every stage's latency, plus every hop's mesh tax. Chapter 9 quantified a real, if small, per-hop overhead; across eight hops in one request, that overhead is additive and has to be budgeted for explicitly, not assumed away. A failure in any one stage needs a stage-appropriate recovery, not a generic one. A dispatch-service instance dying mid-request needs the mesh's retry/circuit-breaking (chapter 9); a downstream consumer of the trip-matched event being temporarily unavailable needs the event backbone's independent-pace fan-out (chapter 10) to hold a backlog rather than block the publisher; a storage write failing in one region needs chapter 17's replication-lag-aware failover, not a simple retry. Debugging a slow or failed request now requires distributed tracing, by construction. With nine stages and eight network hops, "where did this request actually spend its time, and where did it actually fail" is unanswerable without chapter 11's per-hop trace spans stitched together by a shared trace ID.

This course has said some version of this sentence in nearly every chapter, and the capstone is where it finally applies to the whole system at once: decomposition doesn't remove failure modes, it distributes and specializes them — trading one big, simple failure mode (the whole monolith goes down) for many small, well- understood ones, each with its own dedicated, previously-derived recovery mechanism. That is a genuinely better trade at Uber's real scale, and it is not free.

Every layer of this system made the same shape of decision — trade a simpler, more centralized property for a more scalable, more isolated one — at a different point in the stack. Seeing them side by side is the actual payoff of a synthesis chapter:

Read the whole table as one argument, not six: at every layer, this course chose availability, isolation, and horizontal scalability over a simpler, more centralized alternative — and named, honestly, exactly what that choice cost. There is no layer in this stack that got scalability for free.

At Uber's real reported scale — millions of trips per day, across thousands of cities — a request's total latency is the sum of every stage's own work plus every hop's mesh tax (§8b). Toggle stages on and off to see which ones actually dominate a realistic end-to-end budget.

These per-stage millisecond figures are an illustrative, first-principles allocation of a request budget across stages this course actually built — dispatch and routing dominate because batching windows (ch. 4) and route computation (ch. 5) are the genuinely heavier operations — not a claimed measured Uber production number for any specific stage.

Uber has not published one postmortem that names every mechanism this chapter touches in a single incident, so this section is honest about that: what follows synthesizes the realistic, industry-documented failure patterns chapters 9, 10, 11, and 17 each already introduced individually, showing how they'd actually compound in one bad day, rather than reporting one specific real Uber event.

A regional demand spike (a major event letting out, chapter 6's surge scenario) drives a burst of trip requests in one region. The dispatch service under that load starts timing out occasionally — not down, just slow, chapter 9's "worse than clean failure" pattern. Callers' retries, even with backoff and jitter, add real additional load; the circuit breaker for dispatch trips in that region, and the mesh begins failing dispatch calls fast rather than queuing them. Meanwhile, the trip-matched events that DID succeed are queued to the event backbone as usual — but one downstream consumer (say, the receipt-generation service, chapter 10) is independently having a slow deployment window, and its consumer lag starts climbing, exactly as chapter 10 predicted for a consumer that falls behind its independent pace. At the same time, the write volume spike is pushing that region's Docstore compaction backlog up (chapter 16), and if the region's health degrades far enough, the failover coordinator (chapter 17) has a real, non-trivial decision to make about whether to promote a replica and accept whatever RPO the current replication lag implies.

Nothing above is invented lore about a specific real Uber outage — every mechanism cited is the real, general technique its chapter derived, and every failure mode is the realistic, industry-documented pattern that class of system produces under load. The lesson a Staff/Principal engineer should take from this synthesis is that at this scale, incidents rarely stay contained to one layer — they propagate along exactly the dependency chain §1 and §5 established, which is precisely why every layer's recovery mechanism has to be independently correct, not just correct in isolation during a clean demo.
This is the question every chapter in this course has been building toward. Think before you reveal.

No single company's exact internal request-orchestration source is fully public. What follows is precise, representative pseudocode of how a request like this is genuinely orchestrated across independently owned services — labeled as illustrative, citing which chapter's mechanism each piece uses.
The orchestration call chain, citing each chapter's mechanism inline:

Notice that every single cross-service call goes through mesh.Call — never a raw network call — which is exactly chapter 9's argument that cross-cutting concerns don't belong duplicated in application code. Notice the idempotency check happens first, before any real work, and the idempotency record happens last, after everything succeeded — a retried request (chapter 13's mobile-network reality) short-circuits to the same already-computed result rather than re-running (and re-charging) the whole pipeline. And notice the trace span wraps the entire function — every downstream call inherits it, which is the only reason chapter 11's tracing can reconstruct this whole request's path after the fact.
Six questions synthesizing the course, then a sequencing challenge on the pipeline itself. Wrong answers explain why they're wrong.

Send a request and watch it animate through all nine stages in real time. Then break any single stage on purpose and watch the exact recovery mechanism its originating chapter built actually engage — a mesh retry reroutes around a dead dispatch instance, an event-bus backlog absorbs a slow consumer without blocking the publisher, and a regional failover reroutes a storage write.

1. Send a clean request first — watch it flow through all nine stages and land in storage inside budget. 2. Toggle "dispatch instance dies", then send again — watch chapter 9's mesh retry reroute to a healthy instance, adding latency but not failing the request. 3. Toggle "a bus consumer stalls", send a few requests, then watch the consumer-backlog counter climb — the publisher (and the rest of the pipeline) is never blocked by it, exactly chapter 10's point. 4. Toggle "home region degrades" and send again — watch the storage stage reroute to a replica region, exactly chapter 17's failover mechanism, and note the failover counter increment.
These have no multiple choice, and they don't point at a next chapter — there isn't one. Formulate a full answer in your head (or out loud), then reveal.

Eighteen chapters, from a 2009 black-car dispatch app to a simulated request that just walked itself through H3 indexing, batched dispatch matching, live routing and surge pricing, an idempotent trip state machine, an asynchronous event backbone, a service mesh, distributed tracing, and a sharded, multi-region LSM-tree storage engine — and, at every layer, the same honest lesson: there is no free scalability, only a considered, examined placement of the same underlying costs. You now have both the internals vocabulary for a real distributed system at this scale, and the hands-on proof, from every simulator in this course, that the pieces actually fit together.
